readerTitle: What's really left when you sell one more coffee?
caseNote: 가상 사례 (카페, 호텔) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 할인과 특가 주문은 가격이 아니라 판매 한 건이 남기는 돈으로 판단한다.
misconception: 20% 할인이면 20% 더 팔면 된다. 원가 이하처럼 보이는 주문은 무조건 손해다.

factChecks.note: 호텔: $150 − $30 = $120, $80 − $30 = $50 × 50박 = $2,500, 120 ÷ 50 = 2.4배. 할인가에서는 카드 수수료가 조금 줄지만 단순화를 위해 객실당 비용을 $30으로 고정했습니다.

cards.title: What's really left when you sell one more coffee?
body: A latte sells for $5. The coffee, milk and cup cost about $1.20.
So you keep $3.80 a cup? Not quite. And a 20% discount costs more than you'd think.

image.label: Latte with its cost split into layers
image.brief: 라테 한 잔을 세로 단면으로 보여주고, 층마다 "Ingredients $1.20", "Card fee $0.15", "Left over $3.65" 라벨. 맨 아래 층(남는 돈)이 가장 두껍게.

cards.title: How many more lattes would a 20% discount need?
body: Each latte costs you $1.20 in ingredients plus a 3% card fee. You're considering a 20% off promotion: $5 becomes $4.
To earn the same as before, how many more lattes do you need to sell?

options.feedback: It feels logical, but the discount comes entirely out of what's left after costs, not out of the whole price.
Right. You used to keep $3.65 per latte. Now you keep $2.68. To make up the gap, you need about 36% more sales. Next card shows the math.
Good instinct that the discount bites harder than it looks. The math comes to about 36%.

cards.title: Follow one latte.
body: With 20% off: $4.00 − $1.20 − $0.12 = **$2.68**. The price fell 20%. What you keep fell 27%.

breakdown.label: Left over
breakdown.detail: Pays for rent, staff, then profit

cards.title: Contribution margin
body: **Contribution margin** is what each sale leaves after the costs that come with that sale, such as ingredients, fees and packaging.
That money "contributes" to the costs that don't change with sales, like rent and salaries. Once those are covered, the rest is profit.
Here it's $3.65 per latte, or 73% of the price.
cards.softwareNote: The costs that come with each sale are mostly servers, payment fees and support, so contribution margins are often above 70%. That's why special deals can still pay off, and why discounts spread so easily.

cards.title: Selling below "cost" can make you money.
body: A company asks for 200 lattes at $3 each for an event on a quiet Tuesday.
Your accountant spreads rent and staff across every cup and says each latte "costs" $4.35. So $3 looks like a loss.
But rent and staff get paid either way. Each $3 latte still leaves $1.71. That's **$342** you wouldn't have earned otherwise.

image.label: Three bars: $1.29 / $3.00 / $4.35
image.brief: 막대 3개 비교. "Costs that come with each latte $1.29", "Offer price $3.00", "Cost with rent and staff spread in $4.35". 가운데 막대가 첫 번째보다 높다는 점을 강조.

cards.title: This thinking has limits.
body: On average, sales must cover more than their own costs, or the rent never gets paid. If every order is a special deal, you're out of business.
Capacity matters too. If the Tuesday order meant turning away full-price customers, each lost $3.65 counts against it.
And customers talk. A deal for one can become the price everyone expects.

cards.title: Now it's a hotel.
body: Your rooms sell for $150 a night. Cleaning, laundry, toiletries and card fees come to about $30 per occupied room.
A tour company offers to book 50 room-nights in your quiet season, if you charge $80. Should you?

options.text: No. $80 is about half price, so it must lose money
options.feedback: Each room still leaves $50 after the costs that come with it. That's $2,500 from rooms that would otherwise sit empty.

options.text: Yes, but only on quiet dates, on terms that can't replace full-price bookings
options.feedback: You keep the extra $2,500 and protect your $150 guests. The real risk isn't the math. It's the low price spreading.

options.text: Yes, and drop the price to $80 for everyone
options.feedback: Each full-price guest would leave $50 instead of $120. You'd need more than twice as many guests to earn the same.

cards.title: Know what each sale leaves behind.
body: Price minus the costs that come with each sale. That one number tells you what a discount really costs and when a low-price deal is still worth it.
**Try it today:** pick your best-selling product. Write down its price, the costs that come with each sale, and what's left.
